system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

# Chapter 4 — 3-Part Chords: Found and Identified!

_Pages 8-8._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. ## Triad vs 3-part 4th intervals

> The triads primarily consist of 3rds
> and 6ths with some 4ths and 5ths, but contain no 2nds or 7ths.While the 3-part 4ths primar-
> ily consist of 4ths and 5ths with some 2nds and 7ths, but contain no 3rds or 6ths. Clearly,
> these two 3-part chords are very different chord types.

**Significance (p. 8).** This passage defines the fundamental interval-content distinction between triads and 3-part 4th voicings, which is the conceptual core of the comparative analysis in this chapter.

## Interval distribution across chord families

> the total available intervals are evenly distributed within each of the five dif-
> ferent chord types in both 3- and 4-part chords. It is also interesting to note that the omis-
> sion of interval types only occurs within particular 3-part chord families (triad; 3-part 4th;
> spread cluster). Finally, the four chord families with the most even distribution are found
> both in 3- and 4-part chords (7th, no3rd; 7th, no5th; TBN I; TBN ID).

**Significance (p. 8).** This observation articulates the structural rule that certain chord families (7th no-3rd, 7th no-5th, TBN I, TBN II) share even interval distribution across both 3- and 4-part voicings, which is a key analytical finding for understanding voicing families.
